messages.subject: Phenotypic integration with fitted values
messages.body_plain:
Hi Geomorph folks,

I am currently working on assessing the degree to which plasticity and transgenerational effects impact phenotypic integration between two ecotypes across four populations. Running the integration analyses with the integration.vrel and compare.Zvrel functions is straightforward with wild caught or F2 individuals. However, I'm running into issues when modelling transgenerational impacts from grandparents, parents, and the current generation on integration. I have modelled the effects of a single generation on craniofacial shape and obtained fitted values from the model to isolate the effects of a single generation on craniofacial shape. I have converted the fitted landmark data to a 3D array and when I run the integration.vrel function it shows an error: Error in if (Re.obs.trans == 1) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed. When I run with debug, it looks like the error is popping up in lines 19-21 of the integration.vrel function. I'm not really sure why the error is popping up but I'm assuming it has something to due to quantifying variance on fitted landmark values.

If anyone has a potential solution or work around that would be amazing. I may try to add a constant to all landmarks and see if that helps solve the problem. But, if it has something to do with how variance is calculated that should have no effect.

Code below:
F2_off_fitted = F2_off_mod$LM$fitted
F2_off_fitted = arrayspecs(A = F2_off_fitted,
           p = 15,
           k = 2)
identifiers = read_csv('F2_Metadata.CSV',
                       col_names = T) %>%
  unite('Ecotype_Pair_Full_Temp',
        Ecotype_pair,
        Full_temp,
        sep = '_',
        remove = F)

F2_off_fit_sub = coords.subset(F2_off_fitted,
                               identifiers$Ecotype_Pair_Full_Temp)

sum(is.na <http://is.na>(F2_off_fit_sub))

vrel_F2_off_fit = Map(function(x) integration.Vrel(x),
                      F2_off_fit_sub)
Error in if (Re.obs.trans == 1) { : missing value where TRUE/FALSE needed

Observed ratio and rate for group are the same but significance now is:

should I update any other package?

messages.subject: Quantifying Facial Sexual Dimorphism
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I was practicing with my dataset to see if I can manage to calculate 'masculinity and femininity' scores. I saw in this group that projecting shape vectors onto regression axis can be helpful in this context. Due to my inexperience in this area, with the help of some studies, I created this script and calculated the scores. And the scores in fact correlates significantly (but negatively) with other male-dependent variables. Additionally, TPS visualizations are also confirmative.

So, I ended up with females higher on 'masculinity' scores. I think it may indicate that the particular shape features captured by the regression coefficients are more pronounced in females. But I am not sure.

What I wonder is,
-Did I conducted this method correctly? Because I feel pretty sure that I missed something.
-When I multiply 'scores' with -1, I get what is expected. Is it appropriate?
-I used "%*%" for multiplying shape matrix with regression coefficients. Is this an appropriate way to 'projecting?
-What is the proper way to confirm if those scores are accurate and interpretable? Regression with coords ~ sex explains about %12 of variation significantly.

As I mentioned above, I was just practicing to learn. So, if there is an apparent flaw on the script or my understanding of the concept, please feel free to share. Also if there is a more suitable approach to quantify facial sexual dimorphism of human faces, I would appreciate if you could share the details with me.

####Shape Vector Projection (An attempt to calculate masculinity/femininty scores)

library(geomorph)
library(ggplot2)

symall <- readland.tps("symall_merged_2.tps")

symallgpa <- gpagen(symall)

### Creating dataframe

symall_gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(coords = symallgpa$coords, sex = symallsex)

# Flattening the 3D array of Procrustes coordinates into a 2D matrix
coords_matrix <- two.d.array(symall_gdf$coords)

# Creating a data frame with sex as a numeric variable
sex_numeric <- as.numeric(symall_gdf$sex) - 1  # Converting to numeric (0 and 1)

####Regressing sex into coordinates

symallfit <- procD.lm(coords_matrix ~ sex_numeric)

#Exporting coefficients

symallfit.rs <- symallfit$coefficients[-1, ] ###Excluding the intercept

# Projecting the shape data onto the sex coefficients to get masculinity scores

masculinity_scores <- coords_matrix %*% symallfit.rs

Thank you,
Fatih

Fatih,

In R, by default the levels of factors are treated alphabetically. However, if your data happen to have an early specimen in a level higher in the alphabet, they appear ‘reversed’ relative to intuition.

Here is an example from a geomorph dataset. The factor ‘site’ in the plethodon dataset has two levels, allopatry and sympatry. However, the first specimen in the dataset happens to be ‘sympatric’. So using a brute-force method to convert this to numeric (as your code had) will put the sympatric first.  See the results of these lines of code to see what I mean:

library(geomorph)

head(plethodon$site)  #first few specimens

levels(plethodon$site)  #the levels

unique(plethodon$site)  #the levels read in order from the dataset

Being aware of the order of levels of the factor in your dataset will help ensure that you are doing things correctly within the R-environment.

messages.subject: Issue with examples of lm.rrpp (package RRPP)
messages.subject_clean: Issue with examples of lm.rrpp (package RRPP)
messages.body_plain:
Dear geomorph community,

I would like to point out an issue related to some differences in the results obtained when working with the "Pupfish" data in the RRPP package, specifically with the lm.rrpp function, as I would like to understand the underlying reasons of those differences.

Specifically, I was reviewing the code from both the lm.rrpp help file and the supplementary material of Collyer and Adams 2018 Methods Ecol Evol. 2018;9:1772–1779. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.13029 to graph the mean of the predicted values with the 95% CI ellipses.

After applying the code from the example and the supplementary material of the cited article, the graph is slightly different from the one presented in there (Figure 2). The linear model and code used is the following:
fit <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ logSize + Sex*Pop, SS.type = "I", data = Pupfish, print.progress = FALSE)

shapeDF <- expand.grid(Sex = levels(Pupfish$Sex), Pop = levels(Pupfish$Pop))
rownames(shapeDF) <- paste(shapeDF$Sex, shapeDF$Pop, sep = ".")
shapePreds <- predict(fit, shapeDF, confidence = 0.95)
plot(shapePreds, PC = TRUE, ellipse = TRUE)

Conversely, when instead of the factors 'Sex' and 'Population' as well as their interaction, a 'group' factor combining both factors is used, that is:
Pupfish$group <- interaction(Pupfish$Sex, Pupfish$Pop)
fit.group <- lm.rrpp(coords ~ logSize + group, SS.type = "I", data = Pupfish, print.progress = FALSE)

shapeDF.group <- expand.grid(group = levels(Pupfish$group))
rownames(shapeDF.group) <- paste(shapeDF.group$group, sep = ".")
shapePreds.group <- predict(fit.group, shapeDF.group, confidence = 0.95)
plot(shapePreds.group, PC = TRUE, ellipse = TRUE)

The graph obtained is exactly as indicated in Figure 2 of the referred article.

I would like to point out that when I apply the code to my data, which have the same structure as the example, the same happens, and I get different representations when I use two factors and their interaction or the resulting groups from their combination (the interaction between them is also significant). I initially expected the same output, but when I noticed the differences I tested it on the example data and found the same pattern and I am not sure how to interpret it.

In case it helps or if it's an issue on my side, I am using R version 4.3.3 and the latest version of the RRPP package (2.0.1) installed from Github today.

Thank you,

Best,

Lucía

Dear Lucía,

Thanks for the alert.  This is indeed a bug and not a conceptual difference that should exist.  The clue that demonstrates a problem (with the former example) is that the two PCs for the plot sum to 100% when it should take 3 PCs to explain 100% of the variation (since there are 4 means and 4-1 = 3).  The second example can be trusted.  In performing the analysis “by hand” (running the script step by step) I have isolated that the problem is in the creation of the model design matrix to calculate least-squares means.  A redundancy is introduced that produces a column with all values the same.  When I override this, the model design matrix is the same as in the second example, which means the results converge.

How this redundancy came to be I am not yet sure.  I will have to find a new solution, and it might take some time.  In the interim, if you need results, please be aware that the single-factor solution works.  The reason it is not an issue is that full model residuals are bootstrapped to make confidence intervals, and the residuals are the exact same with either approach.  The bug is in the estimation of coefficients with an erroneous model design matrix, which is triggered by the multiple factors.

Silent mutations are the worst for coding (bugs that introduce errors do not produce erroneous results).  This slipped past my radar.  I can fix it now that I know the issue exists, so I appreciate the alert.

Best wishes,
Mike

Kathleen,

There are several ways you can go. One is to read the .fcsv files into geomorph directly using the “readland.fcsv” function.

Alternatively, one can read in data as TPS, NTS, CSV or as a data table. Then, one can simply specify which landmarks are fixed, which are semilandmarks on curves, and which (for 3D data) are semilandmarks on surfaces. To identify the curve points, one creates a ‘slider’ matrix, which specifies which points are curve points, and which points they slide in between. Surface points are just identified by a vector of numbers.

If you look at the help file for gpagen (i.e., type ?gpagen) you will see descriptions of how these are provided to gpagen for Procrustes analysis. Also, at the bottom there are examples. The ‘hummingbirds’ dataset has 2D data with fixed points and curvepoints (meaning it also has the ‘slider matrix’). The 3D example ‘scallops’ has fixed points, curves, and surfaces and the various components specified.

These should be helpful as you work up your dataset in R and in geomorph.

Best,

Dean

The $LM object of the returned variable will contain the fullset of specimens (and landmarks) that you included in the GPA. You can pass that object to gpagen() and do your sliding....

You can install the SlicerMorphR with the devtools: devtools::install_github('SlicerMorph/SlicerMorphR')

and then see a worked example: https://github.com/SlicerMorph/Tutorials/blob/main/GPA_3/parser_and_sample_R_analysis.md

messages.body_plain:
Dear group members,

I would like to ask how does the interpretation of the results of the two-block PLS analysis differs when comparing gomorph (R) and MorphoJ?
The correlation coefficient and p-value of the permutations are the same when testing the same data, however, MorphoJ additionally shows "RV coefficient" and "Singular value" in the results. On the other hand, geomorph displays Effect Size (Z) in the results. The help files for both programs provide basic descriptions of these outputs. However, does the geomorph package contain any equivalent of the aforementioned output from MorphoJ?
And let me ask you one more question that I have not yet been able to find an answer to. Is there any way to extract residuals from PLS analysis, or is there even a need to check for homoscedasticity in this method? I assume that general assumptions (such as data normality, homogeneity or homoscedasticity of residuals) have a slightly different position in the case of  landmark-based data using GMM methods compared to "normal" data and statistical tests?

Best regards,
Miloslav Petrtýl

Dear Miloslav,

The reason we do not report the RV coefficient is because even though it can be used as a test statistic, it is a poor effect size (it’s value changes inherently with different sample sizes and numbers of variables).  This is something we discuss here:

Adams, D. C., & Collyer, M. L. (2016). On the comparison of the strength of morphological integration across morphometric datasets. Evolution, 70(11), 2623-2631.

The Z-score is consistent across different sample size and numbers of variables, so it makes more sense.  One could argue that Pearson product-moment correlation coefficient (calculated on projected PLS scores for the first singular axes) is arbitrarily chosen as a test statistic, when RV could be used (and the two do produce slightly different results), but at least this statistic is computed based on obtaining the major axis of covariation between matrices, meaning it is maximized if the covariance between matrices is maximized.  So it is just mathematically more palatable.

Regarding residuals, this is not a linear regression.  However, the Pearson correlation is the same as finding a major axis regression of projected scores, so one could view residuals by performing such a regression on first X and Y scores.  Yes, a normality assumption is in place for the correlation coefficient.  One could just visualize the plot to see if something is amiss.  Points should be normally distributed along the best fit line that is produced.

If you wish to have an RV coefficient, it is a simple calculation (between X and Y matrices):

RV <- function(X, Y){
  X <- scale(X, scale = FALSE)
  Y <- scale(Y, scale = FALSE)
  sx <- svd(crossprod(X))
  sy <- svd(crossprod(Y))
  sxy <- svd(crossprod(X, Y) %*% crossprod(Y, X))
  sum(sxy$d) / sqrt(sum(sx$d^2) * sum(sy$d^2))
}

There are also some R packages that have functions but you should be weary of significance tests, since they likely assume independent variables, which is not the case for coordinates of landmarks.

Best,
Mike
